title: npm, pnpm and yarn: installing, versioning and publishing packages

videos.script:
Almost no JavaScript program is written alone. {{registry}} Somewhere there is a registry, a server full of packages other people published, and a single command fetches one into your project. That is how a function written once in someone else's library ends up in thousands of programs.

{{json}} The record of what your project depends on is a file called package.json. It names each package and the versions you are willing to accept. {{ranges}} Those versions are written as ranges, and the rules for ranges are what keep an update from breaking your code on a Monday morning.

{{lock}} Then there is the lockfile, which writes down exactly what was installed, so that your laptop, your colleague's laptop and the build server all get the same thing.

{{three}} You will meet three managers that read the same package.json: npm, pnpm and Yarn. They disagree about where packages live and who may import them, and the disagreement is worth seeing.

{{scripts}} You will also see an install run code from a package, and the switches that stop it. {{publish}} And at the end you will publish a package of your own. All of it happens against a private registry that you run on your own computer, so nothing here touches the public one.
